sections.content: A unit like this one surveys a whole royal line, and the natural tool for that is the relative clause: 'X, who did Y, ...'. In Hungarian, the relative pronoun for a person is 'aki' ('who'). It refers back to a person already named in the sentence and introduces a clause that adds information about them — exactly how you'd describe a king in a naturalization interview.

sections.title: aki and akik
rows: who (referring to more than one person)
which, that (referring to things — you'll meet this next lesson)

items.spanish: I. László, aki 1077-től 1095-ig uralkodott, megvédte az ország határait.
items.english: Ladislaus I, who ruled from 1077 to 1095, defended the country's borders.

items.spanish: Könyves Kálmán, aki eltörölte a boszorkánypereket, tudós királyként vonult be a történelembe.
items.english: Coloman the Learned, who abolished witch trials, went down in history as a scholarly king.

items.spanish: II. András volt az a király, aki kiadta az Aranybullát.
items.english: Andrew II was the king who issued the Golden Bull.

sections.content: 'aki' always matches its antecedent in number: one king takes 'aki', several kings take 'akik'. The clause is set off by commas on both sides, and — unlike English, where 'who' can sometimes be dropped ('the king I mean') — Hungarian never drops 'aki'. The verb inside the aki-clause is conjugated for whatever role the person plays inside that clause, which for now is always the subject: 'aki uralkodott' (who ruled), 'aki eltörölte' (who abolished).
